newsitem.title: USA: Simpson jury starts first full day of deliberations.
newsitem.headline: Simpson jury starts first full day of deliberations.

text.p: Jurors in O.J. Simpson's civil trial began their first full day of deliberations on Wednesday to decide if the ex-football star was responsible for the murders of his ex-wife and her friend.

The seven-woman, five-man jury deliberated for about two hours on Tuesday after receiving instructions from Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki, who told them to ignore the fact that Simpson was cleared of the June 12, 1994, murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman by a criminal court jury in October 1995.

The jurors were also directed to disregard the recent ruling of a family court giving Simpson custody of his two children, Sydney and Justin, who had been living with Nicole Brown Simpson's parents, Lou and Juditha Brown.

By mid-morning on Wednesday, the jury had already deliberated longer than the four hours it took the criminal court jury to reach its not guilty verdict. Simpson is battling a wrongful death lawsuit brought by the families of the victims, who are seeking substantial damages.
As the jury met, there was a brief hearing in the judge's chambers in which he granted a plaintiffs' motion forcing the defence to disclose more of Simpson's financial assets.

The jury of nine whites, one Asian-black, one Hispanic and one black, armed with a stack of notebooks in which they wrote during the three months of testimony and a copy of Fujisaki's instructions, have a complicated task in front of them.

First they must decide if Simpson "willfully and wrongfully" caused Goldman's death. If the answer is yes they must then decide if he committed "battery" against Goldman and if that was accompanied by "malice" and "oppression."

But the jurors are not being asked to decide whether Simpson was responsible for the murder of his ex-wife. Instead they are being asked to find if he committed battery against her -- legalese for attacked her -- and if oppression and malice were involved.

According to the judge's instructions, oppression involves an attack on Nicole Brown Simpson that was carried out in a "base, vile, contemptible, wretched, loathsome or miserable" manner that ordinary people would "recoil from."

While Goldman's father, Fred, is suing Simpson on behalf of the family, Nicole Brown Simpson's father, Lou, is suing as executor of his daughter's estate, the beneficiaries of which are Simpson's two young children.

Under California law, an estate cannot sue for wrongful death. It can, however, sue for actual and punitive damages. The actual damages are $250 for the cost of the black dress Nicole Brown Simpson was wearing when she was murdered.
In Goldman's case the actual damages are $100 for the jeans and shirt he was wearing.

Should the jury decide Simpson is liable, it will also have to assess compensatory damages in the case of the lawsuits brought by Fred Goldman and Sharon Rufo, the dead man's natural mother, for "loss of love, affection, companionship and support." But because Nicole Brown Simpson's estate is not suing for wrongful death there will be no compensatory damages in that suit.
If Simpson is found liable there will be a hearing on his worth to help the jury decide what punitive damages should be awarded to the plaintiffs, including Nicole Brown Simpson's estate.

Unlike a criminal trial, the jury does not have to be unanimous and may decide the case by a 9-3 majority. Also it only has to find on the basis of a "preponderance of evidence" rather than "beyond a reasonable doubt."
